land.text: Thomond, 'ruled by the O Briain': 'in much later times' equivalent to County Clare, with parts of Limerick and Tipperary (Thomond article)
Desmond, 'ruled by the Mac Carthaigh': all of County Cork and most of County Kerry (Desmond article)

successors.note: The pages do not say where Waterford and South Tipperary went in 1118.

capitals.name: Cashel
capitals.note: 'the Rock of Cashel became a seat of power' in the Eoganacht period; the infobox lists Cork. No years given; 600 is the researcher's bridge.

correction.text: the province of Munster, 'the territory of the Clanna Dedad' (Erainn)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe; Cliopatria has no Munster. Infobox 'Established: 1st century BC', 'Disestablished: 1118', no area. The page names no counties for the early kingdom; Munster is the six southern counties. The Corcu Loigde 'fell from power' in the 6th century.

correction.text: Munster with Osraige, which 'remained a tuatha of Munster until the 9th century'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Osraige (Kilkenny) was under Munster's control 'for about two centuries'; the page gives no start, so 600 is a bridge (confidence 1) and the end is the 9th century.

correction.text: Munster after Osraige 'was retaken by the Dal Birn'; Brian of the Dal gCais 'established himself not only as King of Munster, but also High King of Ireland'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the province to the partition. The Leinster article says the Laigin 'regained control of Osraige' in the 9th century; this page says the Dal Birn retook it. 900 rounds 'the 9th century'.

region.text: Munster, the Erainn kingdom of the Clanna Dedad

ledger.note: The kingdom of Munster: infobox 'Established: 1st century BC' (legendary); the Corcu Loigde fell from power in the 6th century and 'By the 7th century, the Eoganachta had eclipsed the Corcu Loigde and all others for hegemony in Munster'. 400 is the researcher's opening of the record (confidence 1).

region.text: Osraige, which was under Munster's control 'for about two centuries'

ledger.note: About 600: Munster holds Osraige. The page gives the span ('about two centuries' to the 9th century), not a start year; 600 is a bridge. The Leinster article says Osraige 'went to the Corcu Loigde, becoming part of the Kingdom of Munster'.

region.text: Osraige, 'retaken by the Dal Birn'; 'remained a tuatha of Munster until the 9th century'

ledger.note: 9th century: Osraige leaves Munster. The page says the Dal Birn retook it; the Leinster page says the Laigin regained it, hence the counterpart. 900 is a rounding of 'the 9th century'.

1118: Munster is partitioned. 'Munster was partitioned into Thomond (ruled by the O Briain) and Desmond (ruled by the Mac Carthaigh)'; High King Toirdelbach O Conchobhair and Tadhg Mac Carthaigh agreed the Treaty of Glanmire 'to divide Munster in two'.
1118: Desmond goes to the Mac Carthaigh. In 1118 Brian O Briain attacked Tadhg Mac Carthaigh at the Battle of Glanmire; 'The Mac Carthaigh won, and Brian died.'

region.text: the province, divided between Thomond and Desmond

ledger.note: 1118: the kingdom of Munster ends. Infobox 'Disestablished: 1118'; succeeded by the Kingdoms of Osraige, Desmond, Thomond and Ormond.

wars.name: Battle of Glanmire and the partition of Munster
wars.outcome: Mac Carthaigh victory at Glanmire; the Treaty of Glanmire divided Munster between O Briain (Thomond) and Mac Carthaigh (Desmond).

certainty.note: No page gives a boundary; the province is the best reading and Osraige moves with the 9th century.

notes: Founding 400 is a bridge: the infobox says 1st century BC, which is traditional. Waterford (a Norse town), Limerick, Cork and Youghal were Hiberno-Norse towns inside Munster; no dossier covers them. Cashel (South Tipperary) is not placed in Desmond or Thomond by any page. Brian Boru's High Kingship and Clontarf are mentioned without dates on the page and are not territorial. The page budget (3 pages) was spent on Munster, Desmond and Thomond.
